ceo-revenue.claim: Revenue at risk today — verified contained, or assumed?
ceo-revenue.what: The revenue exposed to today’s active cyber situation, and whether it is genuinely contained — translated into business terms the CEO can act on.

questions.q: “Contained” — verified, or assumed?
questions.a: Verified. The event is held on a compensating control and claims are processing, so the realized revenue rate at risk right now is $0/hr — not an assumption that it’s fine.

questions.q: What revenue and how many customers were ever at risk?
questions.a: The exposed path is claims / payments — worth up to $2.3M/hr if it halted. It did not halt; containment held before any member-facing impact.

questions.q: If containment fails, what’s the exposure?
questions.a: A full claims outage runs to roughly $72M/day in the modeled worst case, plus SLA penalties and member abrasion. That tail is why the remediation decision is on the board page.

ceo-revenue.why: Contained because claims are processing on a compensating control — realized rate $0/hr — even though the exposed path is worth up to $2.3M/hr if it halted.

scenarios.impact: $0/hr becomes $2.3M/hr, up to ~$72M/day
scenarios.body: The compensating control gives way and claims stop. Realized revenue-at-risk jumps from zero to $2.3M/hr, heading toward ~$72M/day — the contained event becomes a revenue event.

scenarios.impact: Claims process slowly; SLA penalties accrue
scenarios.body: Not a full stop but a slowdown. Throughput drops below SLA, penalties and member abrasion accrue — revenue leaks rather than stops.

scenarios.impact: The underlying gap reopens the exposure
scenarios.body: Containment holds now but the root cause (privileged path) is unfixed. The same revenue exposure returns until the remediation lands.

ceo-revenue.aggregate: If realized, "contained" becomes a $2.3M/hr-to-$72M/day revenue event — which is why containment is reported as verified-and-conditional, with the tail visible.
ceo-revenue.tells: “Contained” is verified, not hopeful — today’s realized rate is $0. The number that matters for the board is the tail if containment fails, kept visible rather than buried.
ceo-revenue.confidence: High on realized · Modeled on tail

ceo-brand.claim: Customer & brand impact — how do we know it’s none?
ceo-brand.what: Whether customers or the brand have been affected — and how we would know — stated as an evidenced negative, not merely an absence of bad news.

questions.q: How do we know “none”?
questions.a: No member-facing outage, no confirmed data exposure, and no customer complaints tied to the event. “None” is an evidenced negative across the signals that would show impact.

questions.q: Which asset matters most to our competitive position?
questions.a: Member trust and the claims / PHI data underneath it. The test we apply is what level of compromise that asset could withstand — and today it is untouched.

questions.q: If this became public, what’s the consequence?
questions.a: Reputational, not operational, today — because nothing is confirmed exposed. That flips the moment PHI is confirmed, which is why the forensic-scope and disclosure calls are the keystones.

scope: Customer complaints tied to the event
ceo-brand.why: None because no member-facing outage, no confirmed exposure, and no complaints tie to the event — an evidenced negative that flips the moment PHI is confirmed.

scenarios.t: PHI exposure is confirmed and disclosed
scenarios.impact: "None" becomes a public trust event
scenarios.body: Forensics confirms member PHI was exposed and disclosure follows. Brand impact moves from none to a headline trust problem — the reputational tail behind today’s clean read.

scenarios.impact: Speculation damages trust before findings land
scenarios.body: Word of an "incident" spreads before scope is known. Brand takes a hit from the narrative, not the facts — which is why comms readiness matters as much as forensics.

scenarios.impact: Customers feel claims friction
scenarios.body: Even contained, a processing slowdown is felt by members. "No impact" erodes if the experience degrades, regardless of data exposure.

ceo-brand.aggregate: If realized, "none" becomes a trust event — reputational, not operational — which is why it hinges on the forensic finding and disclosure, and why those calls are the keystones.
ceo-brand.tells: “None” is evidenced across the signals that would show customer impact — not just an absence of complaints. The risk is reputational and hinges on the forensic finding.

ceo-material.claim: Material events — zero confirmed, or zero determined yet?
ceo-material.what: Whether any cyber event has reached the materiality bar this period — and whether the process behind “zero” is sound, because the CEO owns the disclosure posture.

questions.q: Zero confirmed, or zero determined-yet?
questions.a: Zero determined material. Today’s event is under review (estimate $0–1.1M, below the line). The trigger is the determination, not the incident — and it is clock-tracked.

questions.q: What threshold auto-escalates to me?
questions.a: Pre-agreed: any incident affecting more than 100,000 records reaches me and the board within 24h; any materiality determination escalates immediately. Set in advance.

questions.q: Could related incidents aggregate into a material one?
questions.a: Yes — the same actor or the open PAM vulnerability recurring could aggregate under SEC rules. Legal is tracking it so a series doesn’t slip the bar unnoticed.

ceo-material.why: Zero determined material; today’s event is under review below the line — "zero" reflects a sound, clock-tracked determination process, not an absence of looking.

scenarios.impact: Board + SEC clock start
scenarios.body: Forensics pushes the event over the bar. The CEO owns a four-day disclosure clock and a board notification — zero becomes one, fast.

scenarios.impact: >100k-record threshold passed without escalation
scenarios.body: An incident quietly crosses the 100k-record line and the auto-escalation misfires. The board learns late — the failure mode the pre-set trigger exists to prevent.

scenarios.impact: Repeat incidents combine over the bar
scenarios.body: Several immaterial events from the same actor aggregate. The CEO faces a material determination on a pattern, not a single event.

ceo-material.aggregate: If realized, "zero" becomes a material event with the CEO owning the disclosure posture — which is why the trigger thresholds are pre-agreed and the determination is clock-tracked.
ceo-material.tells: “0” reflects a sound, timely process with pre-set triggers — not an absence of looking. The CEO owns the posture, so the escalation thresholds are agreed in advance.

ceo-posture.claim: Posture trend — what does 82 mean, and is the gain real?
ceo-posture.what: The enterprise security-posture score and its direction — what “82” represents, how it compares to peers, and whether the improvement is real.

questions.q: 82 of what — and how do we compare to peers?
questions.a: A weighted roll-up across nine security domains, 0–100. 82 is top-quartile for Fortune-50 healthcare payers on a same-framework basis; recovery and AI governance are the two domains pulling it down.

questions.q: Is the +4 real reduction, or easier targets?
questions.a: Real — driven by control-validation gains (1,238/1,240) and identity improvements, on a four-quarter trend with thresholds that still flag claims as over its line.

questions.q: Is security enabling the business, or just defending it?
questions.a: Both — a defensible posture is what lets us pursue AI and digital initiatives without taking risk over appetite. The score is a means to enablement, not a trophy.

ceo-posture.why: 82 is a top-quartile, four-quarter-improving roll-up — real because it is driven by validated controls, with recovery and AI governance named as the drags.

scenarios.t: A drag domain causes the loss
scenarios.impact: Recovery or AI-gov gap becomes the breach
scenarios.body: The very domains pulling 82 down — recovery, AI governance — are where the next incident lands. A good headline score does not protect the weak domains it is averaging over.

scenarios.t: Score rises while real risk does not
scenarios.impact: Easy-domain gains flatter the number
scenarios.body: Improvements cluster in already-strong domains. 82 ticks up while the load-bearing weaknesses persist — the gaming risk the board should probe.

scenarios.impact: Top-quartile slips as peers improve
scenarios.body: Peers invest and the bar rises. A static 82 quietly drops out of the top quartile — position is relative, not absolute.

ceo-posture.aggregate: If realized, a healthy 82 masks a loss in its weakest domain or a slipping peer position — which is why the score is shown with its drags and its trend, not as a trophy.
ceo-posture.tells: 82 is top-quartile and the +4 is a real, defensible gain — with the two drags named (recovery, AI governance). A score that hid its weak domains wouldn’t be worth reporting.

cro-overappetite.claim: Risks over appetite — which one, and how far over?
cro-overappetite.what: How many individual risks sit above their own board-approved appetite line right now — named, sized, and owned. One over its line does not mean the enterprise is over.

questions.q: Which risk is over, and by how much?
questions.a: Claims processing. Its modeled residual ($94M) exceeds its own sub-appetite line. It is the single contributor over its limit — every other domain is within. Owner: CISO, with the PAM + recovery remediations funded and tracked.

questions.q: Is one-over-appetite a breach I must escalate?
questions.a: Not an enterprise breach — aggregate is still within the $120M line (diversification holds). But a single KRI over its limit is a board-notify item under our RAG rules, which is why it is on this page and not buried.

questions.q: What would push more over?
questions.a: A correlated event — claims + NASCO (third-party) + the ungoverned AI model moving together. The model treats them as independent; if they correlate, the aggregate crosses $120M. That fragility is the real watch, not the single over-line item.

scope: Risks above their own appetite line
How far over, and the owner
Whether it is an enterprise breach
cro-overappetite.why: One — claims — is over its own sub-line ($94M), while the enterprise aggregate stays within $120M; flagged as a board-notify item under the RAG rules even though it is not an enterprise breach.

scenarios.impact: Claims loss lands while it is already over
scenarios.body: The one risk over its line is exactly the one that fires. Being over appetite was not theoretical — it was the warning that preceded the loss.

scenarios.impact: Two over together breach the aggregate
scenarios.body: Third-party or AI crosses its line in the same event as claims. Two correlated breaches push the enterprise aggregate over $120M — the diversification failure.

scenarios.impact: Claims stays over quarter after quarter
scenarios.body: PAM and recovery slip and claims stays over its line indefinitely. A standing breach normalizes — the slow erosion of the appetite framework’s meaning.

cro-overappetite.aggregate: If realized, the one risk over its line is the one that breaches — which is why a single over-appetite item is a board-notify event, not a rounding detail.
cro-overappetite.tells: “1” is honest, not alarming — it names the single risk over its line (claims) while the enterprise stays within appetite. The danger is correlation, not the count.

cro-airisk.claim: AI & agentic risk — how fast is it rising, and is it governed?
cro-airisk.what: Where AI and autonomous-agent risk sits as a contributor to enterprise cyber risk, how fast it is growing, and whether governance is keeping pace.

questions.q: How fast is it rising, and is it governed?
questions.a: It is the fastest-growing contributor — already 16% of aggregate risk and climbing. Governance is partial: an AI inventory exists, but model-access controls and an approval gate are not yet complete (one of the two posture drags).

questions.q: Where will it rank?
questions.a: 3rd-largest contributor today; on the current slope it becomes the single largest within ~12 months if left ungoverned — shifting the risk distribution toward the least-controlled domain.

questions.q: What’s the KRI, and who owns it?
questions.a: KRI: ungoverned / shadow-AI systems with access to PHI or production. Thresholds: green 0, amber 1–3, red 4+. Owner: CISO plus a named AI-governance lead. Currently amber.

scope: The AI KRI and its threshold
cro-airisk.why: Rising — already 16% of aggregate and the fastest-growing contributor — because governance (model-access controls, an approval gate) lags the pace of adoption.

scenarios.t: An ungoverned model is breached or misused
scenarios.impact: Shadow AI with PHI access is exploited
scenarios.body: An agent or model with production/PHI access — outside governance — is compromised or manipulated. The least-controlled domain becomes the breach path.

scenarios.impact: 16% grows to #1 within a year
scenarios.body: Left ungoverned, AI overtakes claims as the largest risk contributor. The risk distribution shifts toward the domain with the weakest controls.

scenarios.impact: Inventory cannot keep up with adoption
scenarios.body: Business units stand up AI tools faster than governance can register them. The KRI goes red as ungoverned systems multiply.

cro-airisk.aggregate: If realized, the fastest-rising risk becomes the breach or the top contributor — which is why an AI-governance gate is the decision this KRI implies.
cro-airisk.tells: “Rising” with a number behind it: 16% and the steepest slope. The decision it implies is an AI-governance gate before it becomes the top contributor.
links: See posture drag from AI governance ▸

cro-trend.claim: Risk trend — improving over what horizon, and are the thresholds real?
cro-trend.what: The direction of aggregate enterprise cyber risk over time, on the board-reported trend — and whether the thresholds behind it are calibrated tightly enough to actually warn.

questions.q: Up over what horizon?
questions.a: Improving four straight quarters on the board-reported trend (the standard ERM view). The arrow is aggregate residual trending down toward appetite, driven by control-validation gains.

questions.q: Are the thresholds real, or too loose to warn?
questions.a: Calibrated to the board-approved appetite, with tiered RAG bands (tolerance / capacity / limit). They are tight enough to have flagged claims as over its line — i.e., warning, not rubber-stamping.

questions.q: When was appetite last reviewed?
questions.a: Reviewed at board level twice a year; the last refresh held the aggregate line at $120M. The claims over-line item is on the next review agenda.

cro-trend.why: Improving four quarters because control-validation gains pull residual down toward appetite — with thresholds tight enough to still flag claims as over its line.

scenarios.t: A single event reverses the trend
scenarios.impact: Quarters of gains erased at once
scenarios.body: The claims exposure realizes and one loss undoes four quarters of improvement. A trend is a trailing indicator — it can reverse faster than it built.

scenarios.impact: Green that no longer warns
scenarios.body: Thresholds are not recalibrated and stop firing — the "green dashboard" failure. The trend looks good because the bar quietly dropped.

scenarios.impact: Trend flattens with claims still over
scenarios.body: Gains stall while the one over-line risk stays over. "Improving" loses meaning if it plateaus above appetite.

cro-trend.aggregate: If realized, an improving trend reverses on one event or on loose thresholds — which is why it is reported four-quarter with calibration that still flags claims.
cro-trend.tells: A trend is only trustworthy if its thresholds can fire — these did, on claims. The arrow is improvement you can defend, not a flattering line.

cro-wirefraud.claim: Wire / payment-fraud exposure — how much is at risk, and is it contained?
cro-wirefraud.what: The modeled 12-month loss exposure from external payment fraud — authorized-push-payment, business-email-compromise, and account-takeover routes into the payments rails — and whether controls hold it within the operational-risk appetite.

questions.q: Where does the $31M concentrate?
questions.a: Authorized-push-payment and BEC against high-value corporate wires — roughly 70% of the exposure. The tail is a single large fraudulent wire clearing before recall.

questions.q: Is it within appetite?
questions.a: Over its own op-risk sub-line. External-fraud capital held ($22M) is below the modeled loss ($31M) — the one category above its line, which is why it sits on this page.

questions.q: What closes the gap?
questions.a: Real-time payee verification plus a hard out-of-band callback on wires over $250K. Funded; rollout is the decision in Decisions Required.

cro-wirefraud.why: Over its line — modeled external-fraud loss ($31M) exceeds the capital held against it ($22M) because real-time payee verification is not yet enforced on high-value wires.

scenarios.t: A single large APP wire clears
scenarios.impact: $8–12M out before recall
scenarios.body: A spoofed payee instruction passes manual review and a high-value wire settles. Cross-border recall fails — the tail event the $31M models.

scenarios.impact: Many mid-size frauds in days
scenarios.body: A credential-harvesting campaign drives a burst of authorized-push-payment fraud faster than ops can triage. Aggregate clears the external-fraud line.

scenarios.impact: $9M gap persists
scenarios.body: Payee-verification rollout is deferred; the category stays over its op-risk line another quarter — a standing breach of appetite.

cro-wirefraud.aggregate: If realized, payment fraud is the one op-risk category over its line that fires — which is why the payee-verification gate is the decision this exposure implies.
cro-wirefraud.tells: $31M is the modeled loss, $22M the capital behind it — the gap, not the headline, is the risk. The decision it implies is a callback gate on high-value wires.

cro-oprisk.claim: Operational-risk capital — are we holding enough against cyber loss events?
cro-oprisk.what: The operational-risk capital allocated to cyber-driven loss-event categories under the Basel operational-risk framework, and whether each category’s capital covers its modeled loss.

questions.q: Is total capital adequate?
questions.a: Aggregate yes — $48M held against $53M modeled, with diversification credit. But one category (external fraud) is individually under-held.

questions.q: Which category is short?
questions.a: External fraud — $22M held vs $31M modeled. Execution / settlement and business-disruption categories are at or within their lines.

questions.q: What drives the number?
questions.a: Internal loss data, scenario analysis, and business-environment factors. The cyber scenarios (ransomware on payments, large APP fraud) are the heaviest contributors.

cro-oprisk.why: Adequate in aggregate ($48M vs $53M with diversification) but one category — external fraud — is under-held, which is the single item over its line.

scenarios.impact: Correlated loss exceeds capital
scenarios.body: A payments-ransomware event and a fraud spike land in the same quarter. Correlated, they overwhelm the diversification credit the capital assumes.

scenarios.t: Loss data revises the model up
scenarios.impact: Capital requirement rises
scenarios.body: New internal loss events push modeled loss above held capital in a second category, forcing a capital add at quarter close.

scenarios.impact: A standing under-hold
scenarios.body: The $9M external-fraud shortfall is not closed; the bank carries a category over its line into the next regulatory review.

cro-oprisk.aggregate: If realized, correlated cyber loss events breach the capital the model assumes is diversified — which is why the external-fraud gap is the one to close first.
cro-oprisk.tells: Capital is adequate in total but thin where fraud concentrates. The honest read is one under-held category, not a system-wide shortfall.

cro-aml.claim: AML / sanctions standing — any open exposure that becomes an enforcement risk?
cro-aml.what: Open anti-money-laundering and sanctions-screening exposures where a cyber or data-integrity failure could degrade detection — and whether any rise to a reportable or enforcement-level concern.

questions.q: What are the two alerts?
questions.a: A screening-system data-feed lag and a transaction-monitoring rule that under-fired after a model change. Neither is a confirmed breach — both are control-health flags.

questions.q: Could cyber make this worse?
questions.a: Yes — degrading or tampering with the monitoring pipeline is a recognized attack path. Detection failure is both a fraud risk and a regulatory-enforcement risk.

questions.q: Is anything reportable?
questions.a: Nothing reportable today. Both items are inside remediation SLAs; the CLO is notified so the disclosure call sits with legal, not buried in ops.

scope: Whether any is a confirmed breach
The cyber path that degrades detection
cro-aml.why: Amber, not red — two control-health flags are open and inside SLA, with no confirmed breach, but a degraded monitoring pipeline is a real cyber-into-compliance path.

scenarios.impact: Illicit flow clears screening
scenarios.body: An attacker or a silent data-feed failure blinds transaction monitoring. Flows that should alert do not — a detection failure that becomes an enforcement matter.

scenarios.impact: A typology goes unflagged
scenarios.body: The post-model-change under-firing is not corrected and a laundering typology passes unalerted until an external trigger surfaces it.

scenarios.impact: Control-health becomes finding
scenarios.body: The two open items slip their remediation SLA and convert from control-health flags into examination findings.

cro-aml.aggregate: If realized, a degraded detection pipeline turns a cyber failure into a sanctions / AML enforcement event — which is why pipeline integrity is monitored as a control, not just an IT asset.
cro-aml.tells: “2 alerts” with zero confirmed breaches is control-health, not crisis — but the cyber path to detection failure is why it sits on the CRO page.

cro-otsafety.claim: OT / safety risk — could a cyber event become a physical or safety event?
cro-otsafety.what: Whether a cyber compromise of operational technology — protection relays, safety-instrumented systems, SCADA / EMS — could cross from data loss into physical consequence: equipment damage, a safety event, or a forced shutdown.

questions.q: Why elevated, not high?
questions.a: The IT / OT boundary is segmented and safety-instrumented systems sit on an isolated network — but remote-access paths into the OT DMZ are not all MFA-gated, which is the one open route to consequence.

questions.q: What is the worst physical outcome?
questions.a: Manipulation of a protection relay or safety system during peak operation — equipment damage and a forced shutdown, with a low-but-nonzero injury risk. This is the tier that separates energy from every other sector.

questions.q: What closes it?
questions.a: MFA on every OT remote-access path and unidirectional gateways on the safety segment. Funded; it is the decision in Decisions Required.

scope: The IT→OT path to physical consequence
cro-otsafety.why: Elevated because segmentation and safety-system isolation hold, but not every OT remote-access path is MFA-gated — leaving one credible route from a cyber intrusion to a physical event.

scenarios.impact: Equipment damage, forced shutdown
scenarios.body: An attacker reaches the OT DMZ over an un-gated remote path and manipulates a protection relay during peak load. The consequence is physical, not informational.

scenarios.impact: Safety function disabled
scenarios.body: A safety-instrumented system is targeted to disable its protective trip — the event the entire safety case exists to prevent. Low likelihood, catastrophic impact.

scenarios.impact: Reliability and safety margin drop
scenarios.body: Ransomware in the OT environment forces a fallback to manual operation, eroding the safety and reliability margin until recovery.

cro-otsafety.aggregate: If realized, a cyber intrusion becomes a physical and safety event — the consequence class no financial or healthcare CRO carries, which is why OT remote-access MFA is the gating decision.
cro-otsafety.tells: “Elevated” is precise: the safety isolation holds, but one un-gated access path keeps a cyber-to-physical route open. The decision it implies is MFA on every OT path.

cro-gridrel.claim: Grid-reliability risk — what does a cyber-driven outage cost, and how likely is it?
cro-gridrel.what: The economic and reliability consequence of a cyber-driven loss of grid operations — a regional outage caused by SCADA / EMS compromise — and where that sits against the board’s tolerance for reliability events.

questions.q: Where does $2.1B/day come from?
questions.a: Regional economic-impact modeling for a one-day loss of dispatch across the served territory — lost load, restoration, and economic knock-on. It is consequence sizing, not a fine.

questions.q: How likely is it?
questions.a: Medium — it requires SCADA / EMS compromise during a stressed grid state. Redundant control centers and manual fallback reduce, but do not eliminate, the path.

questions.q: What reduces it?
questions.a: EMS hardening, control-center redundancy testing, and black-start exercises. The residual is held within the reliability tolerance the board set.

scope: Economic impact of a one-day outage
cro-gridrel.why: Sized at $2.1B/day of economic consequence with medium likelihood — high enough to matter because EMS compromise at peak load is a credible path, low enough to be within tolerance given control-center redundancy.

scenarios.impact: Regional outage, $2.1B/day
scenarios.body: Control of dispatch is lost during a stressed grid state. The outage cascades regionally before manual fallback restores load — the headline consequence.

scenarios.impact: Failover does not save you
scenarios.body: Both control centers run the same un-patched EMS software; the attack that takes one takes both. Redundancy assumed, not achieved.

scenarios.impact: Outage hours extend
scenarios.body: Black-start and restoration take longer than exercised under real conditions, extending the outage and its economic toll.

cro-gridrel.aggregate: If realized, a cyber event becomes a regional outage measured in billions per day — which is why EMS hardening and tested redundancy are reliability controls, not IT projects.
cro-gridrel.tells: $2.1B/day sizes the consequence, not a fine — the number that makes grid reliability a board-tolerance line, with medium likelihood held down by redundancy.

cro-nerc.claim: NERC CIP exposure — any control lapse that becomes a penalty?
cro-nerc.what: Open or at-risk NERC CIP control obligations on BES (bulk electric system) cyber assets, and the regulatory-penalty exposure if a lapse is found — up to roughly $1M per violation, per day.

questions.q: Is anything currently in violation?
questions.a: No confirmed violation — but two CIP controls (a patch-management evidence gap and an access review overdue by 9 days) are at risk and inside remediation windows.

questions.q: Why size it at $1M/day?
questions.a: That is the statutory ceiling per violation per day. The point is not the maximum — it is that an evidence gap on a BES cyber asset is a direct financial exposure, not just a control finding.

questions.q: What clears it?
questions.a: Close the patch-evidence gap and complete the overdue access review. Both are owned with dates; the CLO holds the disclosure call if either slips.

scope: Whether any is a confirmed violation
cro-nerc.why: At risk, not in violation — two CIP controls sit inside remediation windows, but an evidence gap on a BES cyber asset carries a direct per-day penalty exposure if found.

scenarios.impact: Penalty clock starts
scenarios.body: A CIP audit lands on the patch-management evidence gap before it is closed. The finding converts a control-health item into a per-day financial penalty.

scenarios.impact: A second at-risk control matures
scenarios.body: The overdue access review is not completed and crosses from at-risk into a self-reportable lapse, compounding the first.

scenarios.impact: Disclosure judgment call
scenarios.body: The team must decide whether to self-report the gap. Self-reporting mitigates penalties but starts a regulatory process — a CLO call, not an ops one.

cro-nerc.aggregate: If realized, a CIP evidence gap becomes a per-day penalty and a self-report decision — which is why CIP control-health is tracked as financial exposure on the CRO page.
cro-nerc.tells: $1M/day is the ceiling, not today’s loss — the signal is that two CIP controls are at risk with zero confirmed violations, kept that way by dated remediation.

clo-disclosure.claim: Disclosure triggered — zero filed, or zero determined yet?
clo-disclosure.what: Whether any cyber incident has been determined material and therefore disclosable this period. The trigger is the materiality determination, not the incident itself.

questions.q: Zero because nothing’s material, or not determined yet?
questions.a: Zero determined material this period. Today’s event is under materiality review (estimate $0–1.1M, below the quantitative line). The determination, not the incident, is what would trigger a filing.

questions.q: Who owns the determination, and is it timely?
questions.a: Co-owned by Legal + Finance, made without unreasonable delay. The current determination is due within ~2h40m — clock-tracked, so there is no drift between discovery and decision.

questions.q: Does a vendor breach trigger us?
questions.a: Yes — a NASCO / third-party breach that materially affects us triggers the same obligation as a first-party one. That path is monitored given the single-source concentration.

clo-disclosure.why: Zero determined disclosable; the trigger is the materiality determination, which for today’s event has not been made — stated as a timely process, not an absence.

scenarios.impact: Disclosure obligation activates
scenarios.body: The determination is made and the four-business-day clock starts. Zero becomes a live filing obligation with nature/scope/timing/impact to draft under pressure.

scenarios.impact: A vendor event becomes our disclosure
scenarios.body: The single-source processor is breached and it materially affects us. The trigger fires on a third-party event — the path that is easy to overlook.

scenarios.impact: Discovery-to-disclosure gap scrutinized
scenarios.body: The call drifts and the gap between knowing and filing widens. Even a correct disclosure looks late — the optics the SEC examines.

clo-disclosure.aggregate: If realized, "zero" becomes a four-day filing obligation — possibly triggered by a vendor — which is why the determination is owned, clock-tracked, and documented under privilege.
clo-disclosure.tells: “0” means nothing has been determined material — stated as a sound, timely process, not an absence of looking. The clock starts on the call, and the call is on schedule.

clo-clocks.claim: Reg clocks running — which one, and how long do we have?
clo-clocks.what: Which regulatory notification clocks are armed right now, when each starts, and how much time remains — across SEC, state, HIPAA, and contractual obligations.

questions.q: Which clock, when does it start, how long?
questions.a: One state breach-notification clock is armed on today’s event. The SEC 8-K clock is not running — it starts only on a materiality determination (four business days from that point), which has not been made.

questions.q: Are other clocks armed?
questions.a: Tracked in parallel: state AG notice (varies 30–60 days), HIPAA (without unreasonable delay, ≤60 days), and contractual notice to partners. None breached; one running.

questions.q: Is the determination documented defensibly?
questions.a: Yes — contemporaneous notes under privilege, so the timeline between discovery and any determination is defensible if examined.

clo-clocks.why: One state clock is armed; the SEC clock is not running because it starts on a materiality determination not yet made — each obligation tracked separately so none lapses.

scenarios.impact: SEC + HIPAA + state converge
scenarios.body: A material determination starts the SEC clock while HIPAA and multi-state clocks run in parallel. Several deadlines converge — the coordination failure that produces missed filings.

scenarios.impact: Notification deadline missed in one jurisdiction
scenarios.body: One state’s shorter window passes unnoticed amid the others. A single missed jurisdiction becomes a regulatory finding.

scenarios.impact: Less time than assumed
scenarios.body: The determination is dated to when materiality was knowable, compressing the remaining window. The clock had less runway than the calendar suggested.

clo-clocks.aggregate: If realized, one tracked clock becomes several converging deadlines — which is why every regime’s clock is mapped and counted down, not just the SEC one.
clo-clocks.tells: The clock that matters — SEC — has not started, because the trigger is the determination, not the incident. The one running (state) is tracked with time to spare.

clo-privilege.claim: Privilege & preservation — asserted, or just claimed?
clo-privilege.what: Whether legal privilege is genuinely asserted over the investigation and materiality analysis, and whether the evidence chain is preserved for both investigation and disclosure.

questions.q: Is privilege actually asserted, and is outside counsel engaged?
questions.a: Yes — the materiality analysis and forensic findings are routed through outside counsel, so privilege is asserted over the work product, not merely claimed.

questions.q: Is the evidence chain preserved?
questions.a: A litigation hold is issued and the forensic evidence chain is preserved and signed — for the investigation and for any disclosure or insurance claim.

questions.q: Is the documentation dual-use?
questions.a: Yes — built for both internal investigation and regulatory disclosure, so we don’t have to reconstruct a defensible record after the fact.

questions.q: Were tabletop exercises run under privilege?
questions.a: Yes — IR tabletops are conducted under privilege, alongside third-party assessments, so the preparation work is protected too.

clo-privilege.why: In place because the analysis runs through outside counsel and a litigation hold preserves a signed evidence chain — protection asserted, not merely claimed.

scenarios.impact: Internal analysis becomes discoverable
scenarios.body: A court or regulator finds privilege was not properly asserted. The candid materiality analysis becomes evidence against the company — the worst outcome of a sloppy process.

scenarios.t: Evidence is not preserved in time
scenarios.impact: Logs roll off; chain breaks
scenarios.body: A hold issues late and volatile evidence is overwritten. The forensic chain has a gap that weakens both the investigation and any claim.

scenarios.impact: Record must be reconstructed under pressure
scenarios.body: Notes were not built dual-use, so the disclosure record is rebuilt after the fact — slower, and less defensible than contemporaneous documentation.

clo-privilege.aggregate: If realized, "in place" becomes pierced privilege or a broken chain — which is why it is asserted through counsel and preserved contemporaneously, not assumed.
clo-privilege.tells: “In place” means asserted through counsel and preserved — not a checkbox. It is what keeps the materiality analysis defensible and out of discovery.

clo-legalrisks.claim: Open legal risks — what are they, and what’s the exposure?
clo-legalrisks.what: The open legal/regulatory risks tied to the current posture, their realistic liability range, and what would escalate them.

questions.q: What are the two, and the liability range?
questions.a: (1) the SEC disclosure exposure tied to today’s materiality call; (2) the third-party / PHI liability if NASCO data is confirmed exposed. Combined realistic range sits within the $0–1.1M incident band today, with a tail tied to mass-PHI exposure.

questions.q: Could related incidents aggregate?
questions.a: Yes — if the same actor or the open PAM vulnerability recurs, SEC aggregation of related incidents could elevate the combined event. Tracking is in place to catch it.

questions.q: What’s our exposure if data is confirmed exposed?
questions.a: Confirmed mass-PHI exposure moves this from the incident band toward the $94M tail and triggers HIPAA + multi-state notification — which is why the forensic-scope decision is the keystone.

scope: The tail if PHI is confirmed
clo-legalrisks.why: Two open risks — disclosure exposure tied to today’s call, and PHI/third-party liability — both within the incident band today, with a tail tied to confirmed mass-PHI exposure.

scenarios.impact: HIPAA + multi-state + the $94M tail
scenarios.body: Forensics confirms mass PHI exposure. Both risks escalate together — HIPAA and multi-state notification plus a move toward the $94M tail. The keystone forensic finding.

scenarios.impact: Disclosure quality becomes litigation
scenarios.body: A late or thin disclosure invites a securities claim. The disclosure risk converts into active litigation over what was said and when.

scenarios.impact: A pattern raises the stakes
scenarios.body: Repeat events from the same actor combine. The liability is judged on a pattern of control failure, not a single lapse.

clo-legalrisks.aggregate: If realized, the two risks escalate together to HIPAA/multi-state exposure and the $94M tail — which is why the forensic-scope decision is the keystone that governs both.
clo-legalrisks.tells: Two named risks, each with a path to escalation — and both hinge on the forensic-scope decision. The number is small today; the tail is not.

clo-decisions.claim: Decisions today — what’s on me, and which is defensible?
clo-decisions.what: The legal decisions awaiting a call right now — framed by defensibility and the cost of getting them wrong.

questions.q: What are the two, and which is more defensible?
questions.a: (1) make or defer the materiality determination; (2) approve privileged forensic scope. Making the determination on schedule — not early, not late — is the defensible path, documented contemporaneously.

questions.q: What’s the cost of getting the call wrong?
questions.a: A wrong or late call invites SEC scrutiny of the gap between discovery and disclosure — the SolarWinds pattern, where the SEC named the CISO personally. The decision is about defensibility, not just timing.

questions.q: Does the CISO have a direct board path?
questions.a: Yes — a direct escalation path to the audit committee, bypassing the CEO if needed, so the board can make the materiality call with full information.

clo-decisions.why: Two decisions — make/defer the determination and approve forensic scope — both judged on defensibility under examination, with the scope call driving the disclosure call.

scenarios.impact: Under- or over-disclosure, both costly
scenarios.body: Call it immaterial wrongly and face enforcement for under-disclosure; call it material wrongly and move markets needlessly. The determination is a high-stakes legal judgment.

scenarios.impact: Disclosure built on incomplete facts
scenarios.body: A narrow scope misses exposure, and the disclosure rests on facts that later change — forcing an amendment and scrutiny.

scenarios.impact: Board decides without full information
scenarios.body: The CISO’s direct line to the audit committee is not exercised and the board makes the call under-informed — the governance gap the path exists to close.

clo-decisions.aggregate: If realized, a wrong determination or narrow scope cascades into enforcement or amendment — which is why both are framed by defensibility and the scope call gates disclosure.
clo-decisions.tells: Both decisions are about defensibility under examination, not box-ticking — and the forensic-scope call drives the disclosure call.

board-control.claim: Management in control — on what evidence?
board-control.what: Whether the board can conclude management has cyber risk in hand — backed by named owners, tested controls, and independent assurance, not a verbal reassurance.

questions.q: On what evidence — not just an assurance?
questions.a: Named owners, tested controls (1,238 of 1,240 validated against live evidence), and an independent assessment — not management’s word. The two failing controls are named (PAM, recovery), which is itself evidence of real control.

questions.q: Is our oversight demonstrable on the record?
questions.a: Yes — quarterly briefings, this quantified posture, and documented decisions create the Caremark duty-of-care record. The board can show it exercised oversight, with dates.

questions.q: Independent assurance, or only management?
questions.a: Both — internal validation plus third-party assessment. The platform assesses and evidences rather than self-attests.

board-control.why: Yes because controls are tested against live evidence (1,238/1,240) with the two gaps named, and oversight is on the record — evidenced, not a reassurance.

scenarios.t: A named gap causes a breach
scenarios.impact: "In control" is tested by the PAM/recovery gap
scenarios.body: The very gaps management named — PAM, recovery — become the breach. "In control" holds only if the named weaknesses are actually closed, not just disclosed.

scenarios.impact: Caremark exposure on a documentation gap
scenarios.body: A claim alleges inadequate oversight and the board’s record is thinner than believed. The duty-of-care defense rests on contemporaneous evidence that must actually exist.

scenarios.impact: No independent check caught the drift
scenarios.body: Reliance on management’s own attestation misses a real degradation. Without third-party assurance, "in control" is self-graded.

board-control.aggregate: If realized, "yes" is tested by whether the named gaps were closed and the oversight record holds — which is why it rests on tested controls and independent assurance, not assertion.
board-control.tells: “Yes” is evidenced — tested controls and named gaps, not a reassurance. Naming the two failures is what makes the “in control” claim credible.

board-material.claim: Material events — zero, and is the process sound?
board-material.what: Whether any cyber event reached materiality this period, and whether the determination process behind “zero” is sound and timely.

questions.q: Zero determined — is the process sound and timely?
questions.a: Zero material determined this period. Determination is co-owned (Legal + Finance), made without unreasonable delay, and clock-tracked — so “zero” reflects a sound process, not a gap in looking.

questions.q: What threshold auto-notifies the board?
questions.a: Pre-agreed trigger points: any incident affecting more than 100,000 records notifies the board within 24h; any materiality determination notifies immediately. Set in advance, not improvised.

questions.q: Have we been briefed on cadence?
questions.a: Yes — substantive cyber briefings at least quarterly, with an annual deep-dive, per NACD guidance.

board-material.why: Zero determined, behind a sound, clock-tracked process with pre-agreed triggers — "zero" the board can rely on because it reflects the process, not an absence of looking.

scenarios.impact: Board notification + disclosure clock
scenarios.body: Forensics pushes an event over the bar. The board is notified and a four-day clock runs — zero becomes a governed disclosure event.

scenarios.impact: >100k-record event does not escalate
scenarios.body: An incident crosses the threshold but the auto-escalation fails. The board learns late — the exact failure the trigger exists to prevent.

scenarios.impact: A series crosses the bar together
scenarios.body: Repeat events combine into a material pattern. The board faces a determination on accumulated risk, not a single incident.

board-material.aggregate: If realized, "zero" becomes a material event the board must govern — which is why the triggers are pre-agreed and the determination process is clock-tracked.
board-material.tells: “0” backed by a defined, timely process and pre-set triggers — the board knows what would escalate to it and when.

board-decisions.claim: Board decisions needed — what’s ours to decide?
board-decisions.what: What genuinely requires a board decision (versus management execution), framed by risk-reduction-per-dollar and the cost of deferring.

questions.q: What’s the board’s decision vs management’s?
questions.a: The board decision is to approve funding and strategy for the claims remediation (PAM + recovery + NASCO failover). Management runs execution; the board governs the capital allocation and the risk acceptance.

questions.q: What’s the risk-reduction-per-dollar?
questions.a: The funded package is the highest reduction per dollar available — it buys down the $94M claims tail and restores VaR headroom. Deferring leaves the one over-appetite item over.

questions.q: What’s the cost of deferring?
questions.a: Each quarter of delay keeps the $94M claims exposure without failover and the tail VaR ($156M) over appetite. Delay is itself a risk-acceptance decision the board is making.

board-decisions.why: One — fund the claims remediation — is genuinely the board’s call (capital allocation and risk acceptance), distinct from the execution management owns.

scenarios.impact: $94M stays un-failed-over another quarter
scenarios.body: The board defers funding. The claims exposure keeps no failover and the tail VaR stays over appetite — a deferral that is itself a risk-acceptance decision.

scenarios.impact: Approval without urgency loses the quarter
scenarios.body: The board approves but does not press on timeline. Execution drifts and the risk reduction the dollars bought arrives late.

scenarios.impact: Capital approved without accepting residual
scenarios.body: The board funds without explicitly accepting the residual that remains. The risk-acceptance half of the decision goes unrecorded — a governance gap.

board-decisions.aggregate: If realized, deferring or under-driving the one decision leaves the $94M exposure open — which is why it is framed as capital-vs-risk with the cost of delay quantified.
board-decisions.tells: One decision, clearly the board’s: fund the remediation or accept the tail. It is framed as capital-vs-risk, not a technical ask.

board-appetite.claim: Posture vs appetite — within the line we approved?
board-appetite.what: Where enterprise cyber risk sits against the appetite the board itself approved, in the same terms as every other enterprise risk.

questions.q: Within the appetite we approved — what’s the headroom?
questions.a: Within the $120M appetite the board set, with $26M headroom on expected loss. One contributor (claims) is over its own sub-line; the aggregate is not.

questions.q: Is cyber shown apples-to-apples with other risks?
questions.a: Yes — expressed in the same annualized-loss dollars as market, credit and operational risk. Cyber is currently the 3rd-largest enterprise risk by residual.

questions.q: What would move us out of appetite?
questions.a: A single uncontained claims event, or correlated contributors — which pushes the tail VaR ($156M) over. The remediation decision is what restores tail headroom.

board-appetite.why: Within the $120M the board set, with $26M headroom on expected loss — honest that the 95th-percentile VaR ($156M) is over at the tail.

scenarios.impact: $156M VaR over the $120M line
scenarios.body: A 95th-percentile claims event realizes. The board hears the number move from within to $156M over appetite — "within" was an expected-loss statement.

scenarios.impact: Independent-looking risks move together
scenarios.body: Claims, third-party and AI couple in one event and the diversification holding the total under $120M fails. The aggregate breaches the appetite the board owns.

scenarios.impact: $26M thins as risk drifts up
scenarios.body: Rising AI and third-party risk thin the $26M headroom until an ordinary event crosses the line. The buffer disappears before the breach.

board-appetite.aggregate: If realized, "within" becomes "over" at the tail or through correlation — which is why the board sees expected and VaR together against the appetite it approved.
board-appetite.tells: “Within” on the appetite the board owns — honest that expected is within and the tail is over. That is the distinction that prevents a surprise.

board-peer.claim: Peer benchmark — against whom, and is it credible?
board-peer.what: How the organization compares to peers — on a credible same-framework basis — and where it is strong versus weak, shown honestly rather than cherry-picked.

questions.q: Benchmarked against whom, and is it credible?
questions.a: Against same-framework Fortune-50 healthcare payers (matched on the same assessment framework, not marketing). Top-quartile on control validation and posture; mid-band on recovery — shown honestly.

questions.q: Does our insurance match our exposure?
questions.a: Only partly — the tower is $75M against a $94M worst case, a ~$19M uninsured tail. Top-quartile posture does not erase the coverage gap; it is a board accept/transfer item.

questions.q: Are we covered on supply chain?
questions.a: This is our weakest peer-relative area — single-source NASCO concentration. The sector has seen a sharp rise in third-party attacks, and our failover gap is the one to close.

board-peer.why: Top quartile overall on a same-framework basis, shown honestly with the weak domains named — recovery, third-party concentration, and the insurance gap.

scenarios.t: The weak domain is where we are breached
scenarios.impact: Third-party/recovery gap, not the strong areas
scenarios.body: The breach lands in recovery or the NASCO concentration — exactly where we trail peers. Top-quartile overall does not protect the below-average domains.

scenarios.t: Insurance gap is exposed in a loss
scenarios.impact: $75M tower vs $94M worst case
scenarios.body: A catastrophic event reveals the ~$19M uninsured tail. Top-quartile posture did not close the coverage gap — a board accept/transfer item.

scenarios.impact: Top-quartile slips to median
scenarios.body: The cohort invests and the bar rises while we hold. Relative standing erodes even as our absolute score holds — position is relative.

board-peer.aggregate: If realized, the breach or loss lands in exactly the domains where we trail — which is why the benchmark names the weak areas (recovery, third-party, insurance) rather than just the rank.
board-peer.tells: Top-quartile overall, but the benchmark is honest about where we trail — recovery and third-party. A benchmark that hid those would be worthless.

cfo-spend.claim: Cyber spend YTD — what did $10.2M actually buy?
cfo-spend.what: Total cybersecurity spend year-to-date — operating plus project. The number a CFO cares about is not the $10.2M; it is the risk it bought down and whether each dollar is working.

questions.q: What’s the return on this spend?
questions.a: $10.2M YTD has reduced modeled annualized loss exposure by ~$148M — from ~$242M inherent to $94M residual. That is a ~14× risk-reduction-to-cost ratio. Watch the $148M it bought down, not the $10.2M.

questions.q: Which controls earn their keep — and which don’t?
questions.a: Highest return per dollar: the PAM rollout ($4.2M), which closes the $94M claims path — the single biggest reduction available. Recovery modernization ($6.0M, funded) is the next-highest leverage. Flagged: legacy DLP ($0.8M) now overlaps the new CASB — redundant, recommend retire.

questions.q: How do we compare to peers?
questions.a: Spend is ~0.42% of revenue and ~5.1% of IT budget — mid-band for a Fortune-50 payer (peer range 0.3–0.6% of revenue). We are neither over- nor under-spending. The question is mix, not size.

questions.q: Is the opex/capex split right?
questions.a: 62% opex (run) / 38% capex (build). The funded roadmap shifts ~2 points to capex next year toward recovery and AI governance — the two domains currently dragging posture.

scope: Spend vs revenue and IT-budget peer bands
cfo-spend.why: $10.2M is defensible because it bought down ~$148M of modeled loss (~14×) and sits mid-band for peers — the question is allocation, not amount.

scenarios.t: Underfunding leaves the claims path open
scenarios.impact: Saving on PAM/recovery exposes $94M
scenarios.body: Spend is trimmed and the PAM + recovery programs slip. The $10.2M looks efficient until the unfunded gap becomes the $94M loss — the false economy of cutting the highest-return controls.

scenarios.t: Spend rises but risk does not fall
scenarios.impact: Budget grows on low-return tools
scenarios.body: Dollars flow to redundant tooling (e.g., legacy DLP) instead of PAM. Spend climbs while residual risk holds flat — the ROI the board should challenge.

scenarios.impact: Trimmed to the bottom of the band, under-protected
scenarios.body: To hit a peer-low ratio, spend is cut below what the risk warrants. The number looks competitive while protection thins under the appetite line.

cfo-spend.aggregate: If realized, the risk is spending more for less or cutting the controls that matter — which is why this is reported as risk-bought-down per dollar, not a raw budget line.
cfo-spend.tells: Spend is appropriately sized against peers; the lever is reallocation, not more budget. The single best next dollar funds the controls behind the two posture drags — recovery and AI governance.
cfo-spend.freshness: Finance actuals through last close · risk model refreshed 14:00
cfo-spend.confidence: High on spend (pulled) · Modeled on risk-reduction
links: See the $94M exposure this bought down ▸

cfo-exposure.claim: Exposure today — is the number whole-company or just this event?
cfo-exposure.what: The bounded, incident-specific financial exposure from today’s contained event — deliberately separated from the enterprise residual so the two are never confused.

questions.q: Is that the whole company, or just this incident?
questions.a: Just this incident’s path — the contained claims/payments event from today. It is not the enterprise number. Enterprise modeled residual is $94M (shown in Material exposure / Loss-vs-appetite).

questions.q: Is $0–1.1M expected or worst-case?
questions.a: It is the range. ~$180K expected (response + notification), $1.1M at the 95th percentile if data scope widens. The 1% tail — confirmed mass-PHI exposure — is modeled separately at up to $94M and lives in Material exposure, not here.

questions.q: What does a day of downtime cost?
questions.a: ~$2.3M/hr if claims halt (SLA penalties + manual processing + member abrasion). But claims are running on a compensating control, so today’s realized rate is $0.

questions.q: Does it threaten covenants or liquidity?
questions.a: No. $1.1M sits inside the contingency budget and well within covenant headroom. No liquidity action required.

scope: Realized cost on the compensating control
cfo-exposure.why: $0–1.1M is the bounded incident range — ~$180K expected, $1.1M at the 95th percentile — deliberately separated from the $94M enterprise tail so "today" is never confused with "worst case."

scenarios.impact: Realized cost jumps from $0 toward $2.3M/hr
scenarios.body: The control holding claims fails and processing halts. Today’s $0 realized rate becomes $2.3M/hr — the incident escalates from bounded to bleeding.

scenarios.impact: $1.1M ceiling gives way to the $94M tail
scenarios.body: Forensics confirms PHI exposure. The incident leaves the $0–1.1M band and joins the enterprise tail — the 1% case the range excluded.

scenarios.impact: $1.1M lands with no budget headroom
scenarios.body: The $1.1M hits when contingency is spent elsewhere. A small, affordable number becomes a real squeeze on the quarter.

cfo-exposure.aggregate: If realized, today’s bounded $0–1.1M escalates to the $2.3M/hr or $94M tail — which is why the incident number is shown separately from the enterprise exposure.
cfo-exposure.tells: The exposure you can be asked about today is bounded and affordable. The number that matters for the board is the $94M tail — deliberately kept separate so “today” is never conflated with “worst case.”

cfo-insurance.claim: Insurance — do our limits match our exposure, or do we just “have coverage”?
cfo-insurance.what: Whether the cyber-insurance tower is adequate against quantified exposure — limits, retention, and what is actually covered — not merely whether a policy exists. “Below” = today’s event is below the claim threshold.

questions.q: Do our limits match our exposure?
questions.a: Partial gap. Tower limit is $75M against a modeled worst-case single event of $94M (claims) — a ~$19M uninsured tail. Coverage is adequate for expected and 95th-percentile losses; the catastrophic tail is under-covered.

questions.q: What’s the retention, and is business interruption covered?
questions.a: Self-insured retention $2.5M. Business interruption is covered (72-hour waiting period). Today’s $0–1.1M event sits below retention — no claim, but preserve the right.

questions.q: Are claim protocols actually in our plans?
questions.a: Yes. Carrier contacts and notice procedures are embedded in the incident-response and DR runbooks — not a separate binder no one opens under pressure.

questions.q: Below threshold, or notify now?
questions.a: Below the mandatory threshold, but a precautionary notice is advised to preserve coverage — no admission, protects the claim. Window closes in ~46h.

cfo-insurance.why: Below the claim threshold today, but the tower ($75M) sits under the modeled worst case ($94M) — adequate for expected and 95th-percentile losses, short on the catastrophic tail.

scenarios.impact: $94M event vs $75M limit = ~$19M uninsured
scenarios.body: A full claims breach realizes at the worst case. Insurance covers $75M and the company absorbs ~$19M plus anything above — the uninsured tail that "have coverage" hides.

scenarios.impact: Coverage exists but pays late or partial
scenarios.body: The carrier disputes scope or timing and the recovery is delayed or reduced. Coverage on paper is not cash in hand when liquidity is needed.

scenarios.impact: $2.5M SIR absorbs the loss, no claim
scenarios.body: A mid-size incident lands below the $2.5M retention. The company eats it entirely — insurance only helps above the line the SIR sets.

cfo-insurance.aggregate: If realized, "below threshold" becomes a ~$19M uninsured tail or a delayed claim — which is why the test is limits-vs-quantified-exposure, not whether coverage exists.
cfo-insurance.tells: “Have coverage” is the wrong test. Limits cover the likely loss but leave a ~$19M tail uninsured — a board-level accept/transfer decision, not a checkbox.
cfo-insurance.confidence: High on terms · Modeled on worst-case

cfo-materiality.claim: Materiality — by what standard, and when does the clock start?
cfo-materiality.what: Whether today’s event is financially material under the reasonable-investor standard — the determination that starts the SEC four-business-day disclosure clock. Co-owned by Finance and Legal.

questions.q: Material by what standard?
questions.a: The reasonable-investor standard — both quantitative (impact on financial condition / results) and qualitative (PHI, reputation). Current estimate ($0–1.1M) is below quantitative materiality; qualitative factors are under review with Legal.

questions.q: When does the clock start, and who owns it?
questions.a: The four-business-day 8-K clock starts on the materiality determination — not on today’s incident. Determination is co-owned by Legal + Finance, due within ~2h40m, and must be made without unreasonable delay.

questions.q: What would we disclose, and is it defensible?
questions.a: If determined material: nature (contained claims-control failure), scope (under forensic review), timing, and impact range ($0–1.1M). Defensible because the determination is documented contemporaneously under privilege.

questions.q: Could aggregation tip it?
questions.a: Watch item. If the same actor or the open PAM vulnerability is exploited again, SEC aggregation of related incidents could move the combined event to material. Tracking is in place.

cfo-materiality.why: Under review because today’s estimate ($0–1.1M) is below the quantitative line, but qualitative factors (PHI, reputation) are still being weighed with Legal — and the clock starts on the determination, not the incident.

scenarios.impact: Gap between discovery and filing draws SEC scrutiny
scenarios.body: The determination drifts and the 8-K files late. The SEC’s focus on the discovery-to-disclosure gap (the SolarWinds pattern) turns a process delay into an enforcement risk.

scenarios.impact: $0–1.1M becomes a disclosable PHI event
scenarios.body: Forensics confirms mass-PHI exposure. The estimate jumps toward the $94M tail and the event crosses the materiality bar — the disclosure the board must get right.

scenarios.impact: Repeat of the same actor/vuln becomes material in aggregate
scenarios.body: The same actor or PAM vulnerability recurs. Individually immaterial events aggregate under SEC rules into a material one — the watch that is easy to miss.

cfo-materiality.aggregate: If realized, "under review" becomes a material event with a four-day clock — which is why the determination is owned, documented under privilege, and clock-tracked from the moment it is made.
cfo-materiality.tells: “Under review” is the honest state — and the clock has not started, because the trigger is the determination, not the incident. The defensibility comes from documenting the call as it is made.

cfo-appetite.claim: Loss exposure vs appetite — within by how much, and on which measure?
cfo-appetite.what: Where modeled cyber loss sits against the board-approved risk appetite — expressed in the same annualized-loss terms as every other enterprise risk so the board can rank them apples-to-apples.

questions.q: Within by how much?
questions.a: Modeled residual annualized loss is $94M against a board-approved appetite of $120M — $26M of headroom (22%).

questions.q: Is that expected loss or the tail?
questions.a: $94M is the expected annualized loss. The 95th-percentile Cyber VaR is $156M — which is over appetite at the tail. “Within” is true on expected loss, tight at the tail.

questions.q: How does cyber compare to our other risks?
questions.a: Shown in the same annualized-loss terms as market, credit, and operational risk so the board can rank them directly. Cyber is currently the 3rd-largest enterprise risk by residual.

questions.q: What would push us over?
questions.a: A single uncontained claims event, or two contributors moving together (claims + third-party). The claims-modernization decision is what restores tail headroom.

cfo-appetite.why: Within because aggregate residual ($94M) sits under the $120M board line on expected loss — but it is "within," not "comfortable," because the 95th-percentile Cyber VaR ($156M) is over at the tail.

scenarios.t: Tail event lands; VaR over appetite
scenarios.impact: $156M tail exceeds the $120M line
scenarios.body: A 95th-percentile event realizes — a single uncontained claims breach. The number the board hears flips from $94M within to $156M over appetite. "Within" was always an expected-loss statement.

scenarios.impact: Independence assumption breaks; aggregate over
scenarios.body: Claims, third-party and AI move as one in a single event. The diversification holding the total under $120M evaporates and the aggregate breaches appetite.

scenarios.t: Headroom erodes as risk drifts up
scenarios.impact: $26M headroom shrinks quarter over quarter
scenarios.body: AI and third-party risk rise faster than remediation. The $26M of headroom thins until an ordinary event is enough to cross the line.

cfo-appetite.aggregate: If realized, "within" becomes "over" — most likely at the tail or through correlation — which is why the CFO view shows expected and VaR side by side, not a single comforting number.
cfo-appetite.tells: “Within” is accurate on the expected number and honest about the tail being over. That distinction — expected vs VaR — is exactly what keeps a board from being surprised.

cfo-decisions.claim: Decisions today — what am I approving, and what does each cost?
cfo-decisions.what: The financial decisions awaiting the CFO right now — each framed as a treatment choice (accept / mitigate / transfer / avoid) with its cost, its risk-adjusted return, and the cost of delay.

questions.q: What are the three, and what do they cost?
questions.a: (1) Authorize $180K incident-response / forensics. (2) File a precautionary insurance notice ($0). (3) Hold or book a contingent loss reserve ($0–1.1M).

questions.q: For each — accept, mitigate, transfer, or avoid?
questions.a: (1) Mitigate — full forensics; risk-adjusted ROI strongly positive: $180K protects a multi-$M insurance claim and the materiality call. (2) Transfer — preserve insurance. (3) Accept / hold — reserve is below materiality; revisit in ~2h40m.

questions.q: What’s the cost of delay?
questions.a: Forensics delay weakens both the insurance claim and the materiality determination. The insurance-notice window closes in ~46h. The reserve decision is tied to the materiality clock.

questions.q: Which touch disclosure, covenants, or audit?
questions.a: The forensics scope drives the materiality / disclosure call (Legal + SEC). The reserve is an audit-committee item. None threaten covenants.

cfo-decisions.why: Three because today’s event forces a forensics spend, an insurance-notice call, and a reserve decision — each a treatment choice with a deadline, and the forensics call gates the other two.

scenarios.impact: Weakens both the insurance claim and the materiality call
scenarios.body: The $180K forensics is delayed. Without scope, the insurance claim weakens and the materiality determination cannot be made defensibly — $180K saved against multi-$M and disclosure risk.

scenarios.impact: ~46h lapses; coverage right is prejudiced
scenarios.body: The precautionary notice is not filed in time. The carrier later contests late notice, putting the claim at risk for a $0-cost action not taken.

scenarios.impact: Too low surprises the audit committee; too high hits guidance
scenarios.body: The contingent reserve is set wrong as facts develop. An under-reserve becomes a later surprise; an over-reserve dents guidance — the audit-committee tension.

cfo-decisions.aggregate: If realized, deferring the forensics decision cascades into the insurance and disclosure calls — which is why the three are shown together with their deadlines, not as separate tickets.
cfo-decisions.tells: Each decision is a financial choice with a treatment, a number, and a deadline — not a technical escalation. The $180K forensics call is the keystone: it gates both the insurance recovery and the disclosure determination.

intrusions.claim: Active compromise — is an adversary in our environment right now?
intrusions.what: Whether any confirmed adversary presence or active intrusion exists across the monitored estate right now. This is the first question a CISO asks every morning — and the one that can’t wait.

questions.q: Is "None" evidenced, or just no alerts?
questions.a: Evidenced. 312,400 events were correlated in the last 24h and zero matched a confirmed-compromise pattern. "None" is a tested negative, not silence.

questions.q: If an adversary were here, how fast would we know?
questions.a: Detection covers 99.4% of the estate, and the two high-severity alerts overnight were triaged to benign. The answer is evidenced across every monitored surface, not assumed.

questions.q: So what isn't fully closed?
questions.a: Nothing active — but the exploitable paths remain (privileged access to claims). "No intruder right now" is not "no way in" — that's what Exploitable exposure tracks.

scope: SIEM-correlated events across all of the above
intrusions.signals: “None” means 0 events matched a confirmed-compromise pattern — not that nothing was looked at. 312,400 events were correlated in the last 24h to get here.
intrusions.why: None because every confirmed-compromise detection pattern returned zero across 312,400 correlated events; the only two unresolved high-severity alerts were triaged to benign; and there are no active threat-intel (IOC) matches. “None” is an evidenced negative, not an absence of looking.

scenarios.t: An intrusion is present but below detection
scenarios.impact: Adversary dwells undetected; "None" becomes a missed positive
scenarios.body: A novel technique slips beneath the 312k correlated patterns and sits under the threshold. The morning answer flips from a tested "None" to undetected presence — the case every CISO fears, and why 99.4% coverage and active hunting matter more than the headline.

scenarios.t: A "benign" alert was actually the foothold
scenarios.impact: One of the two triaged alerts was the real entry point
scenarios.body: An alert scored benign overnight was a genuine foothold. Dwell time accrues before re-triage catches it — turning a clean board into an active incident and starting the materiality clock late.

scenarios.t: Coverage gap on the un-instrumented estate
scenarios.impact: Intrusion lands where there is no telemetry to see it
scenarios.body: The ~0.6% of the estate outside EDR/SIEM is exactly where an adversary can operate unseen. "None" is only as good as coverage; the un-instrumented slice is the blind spot to close.

intrusions.aggregate: If any realized, the daily "None" becomes an undetected active intrusion — the worst case for a CISO — which is why the answer rests on 99.4% coverage and continuous hunting, not the absence of alerts.
intrusions.tells: The single most important morning answer: no adversary is currently operating inside the estate. It does not mean invulnerable — it means no active intrusion right now, evidenced across every monitored surface.

controls.claim: Critical controls validated — are my defenses actually holding?
controls.what: How many critical security controls passed automated validation against live evidence in the latest cycle — and which two did not. This is control efficacy proven by test, not by a policy document saying the control exists.

questions.q: Validated how — tested, or self-attested?
questions.a: Tested against live telemetry (EDR, SIEM, PAM, identity, scanning) — not a policy document saying the control exists. Each of the 1,240 is exercised against real evidence.

questions.q: Which 2 failed, and do they matter?
questions.a: Privileged access (PAM, 60% deployed) and recovery planning (DR test overdue). Not random — they're the exact controls behind the #1 exposure (claims) and the recovery drag on posture.

questions.q: Isn't 99.8% good enough?
questions.a: It's strong — but the value is in naming the 2 that failed, because both are load-bearing for the biggest risk. A 99.8% that hid which two failed would be worthless.

scope: Validated against live telemetry (EDR, SIEM, PAM, identity, scanning)
controls.signals: Each control is exercised against real evidence and must produce a passing signal. 1,238 passed; 2 failed — and the 2 that failed are the ones that matter.
controls.why: It is 1,238 of 1,240, not all green, because two critical controls are failing on live evidence: privileged access (PAM) is only 60% deployed, and recovery planning (DR test) is overdue. Those two aren’t random — they are the exact controls behind the #1 exposure (claims) and the recovery drag on posture. The system surfaces the two that matter rather than burying them in a 99.8% pass rate.

scenarios.t: The PAM gap is exploited before closure
scenarios.impact: The failing control is the one that gets used
scenarios.body: The 40% of privileged access not yet under PAM is the exact path to claims. The failing control is not cosmetic — it is the enabler of the $94M exposure, used before the rollout finishes.

scenarios.t: Recovery is needed before the DR test is done
scenarios.impact: Unproven recovery → 4.3-day restore vs 4-hour RTO
scenarios.body: An incident forces recovery while the DR test is still overdue. Restore takes 4.3 days against a 4-hour RTO — the failing recovery control turns a containable event into a multi-day outage.

scenarios.impact: One of the 1,238 degrades between cycles
scenarios.body: A control that passed last cycle quietly breaks before the next. Without continuous validation it shows green while failing — which is why these are tested against live evidence, not attested.

controls.aggregate: If realized, the two failing controls are precisely the ones that convert the #1 exposure into a loss and stretch recovery to days — which is why naming them beats a 99.8% pass rate.
controls.tells: Whether your defenses work in reality, not on paper. 1,238/1,240 is strong — but the value is in naming the 2 failures, because both are load-bearing for the biggest risk. A 99.8% that hid which 2 failed would be worthless.

blocked.claim: Attacks blocked, last 24h — is the perimeter doing its job?
blocked.what: Malicious attempts stopped by identity and perimeter defenses in the trailing 24 hours, by category — proof the controls are actively earning their keep, and a read on what’s being thrown at you.
blocked.signals: 4,102 blocked of 4,118 hostile attempts. The 16 that weren’t auto-blocked were escalated to review — all benign.
blocked.why: 4,102 is high because identity is under constant pressure: 3,540 of the blocks were credential/MFA attacks, meaning attackers are overwhelmingly going after logins, not the perimeter. 99.6% were stopped automatically; the 16 escalations were reviewed to benign. The shape of this number — identity-dominated — tells you where the fight is.
blocked.tells: Two things: the controls are working (99.6% auto-blocked), and the threat is identity-led (86% of blocks were credential attacks). That second read is why identity and MFA get the investment — the data says that’s where attackers are.

ciso-vulns.claim: Critical unpatched vulnerabilities — exploitable and exposed
ciso-vulns.what: Critical-severity vulnerabilities still unpatched on in-scope assets — prioritized by whether they are actually exploitable and reachable, not by raw CVSS score. The question isn’t how many; it’s how many an attacker could use today.

questions.q: Why only 2 — we have far more open CVEs?
questions.a: Because these are prioritized by exploitability and reachability, not raw CVSS. Of all open findings, 2 are externally reachable and 1 is on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list — the ones usable today.

questions.q: Is the KEV one being exploited in the wild?
questions.a: KEV means it is actively exploited somewhere. It's inside SLA for emergency patching and is the top remediation priority — tracked to closure, not just logged.

questions.q: What's the business path if it's used?
questions.a: Each maps to an asset and what it reaches. The concern is any that shortens the path to the claims database — that's the link between a vuln and the $94M exposure.

scope: All production assets in the CMDB
Critical CVEs (CVSS ≥9 or on the CISA KEV list)
Flagged if internet-facing or on a crown-jewel system
Ranked by exploit-likelihood (EPSS), not severity alone
ciso-vulns.signals: 7 critical unpatched — but they are not equal. We rank by exploitability × exposure × asset criticality, which is what turns “7” into a real priority list.
ciso-vulns.why: Of the 7, two are internet-facing and one of those is on the CISA Known-Exploited-Vulnerabilities list — actively exploited in the wild, and its 14-day patch SLA is breached. Those two are the real risk. The other five are internal, behind segmentation, and within SLA. The headline number is 7; the number that should set your day is 2 (or really 1).

scenarios.t: The KEV vuln is exploited before patch
scenarios.impact: Known-exploited bug used against an internet-facing asset
scenarios.body: The CISA-listed KEV is weaponized in the wild and our internet-facing asset is unpatched past SLA. This is the highest-probability path to initial access — which is why it is the top priority, not buried in a CVSS list.

scenarios.t: External vuln chains to the claims path
scenarios.impact: Initial access bridges to the $94M exposure
scenarios.body: One of the two externally reachable vulns becomes the entry point that, via the open PAM gap, reaches claims. Two ordinary-looking vulns become the first link in the chain to the biggest risk.

scenarios.impact: A "low" vuln becomes exploitable overnight
scenarios.body: A vuln scored low today is added to KEV tomorrow as exploit code drops. Exploitability is a moving target; the watch is continuous re-prioritization, not a one-time scan.

ciso-vulns.aggregate: If realized, these two are the initial-access step that, through the privileged-access gap, reaches the $94M claims exposure — which is why exploitability, not raw count, is the metric.
ciso-vulns.tells: Where an attacker could get in today. The value isn’t the count — it’s the prioritization: “2 internet-facing, 1 actively exploited, SLA breached” is your patch-now list, and it’s defensible to anyone who asks why those and not the others.

ciso-attacksurface.claim: Internet-facing exposed assets — your external attack surface
ciso-attacksurface.what: Everything of yours reachable from the public internet — the surface an external attacker can actually see and probe — with anything misconfigured, unmanaged, or newly-appeared flagged. You can’t defend what you don’t know is exposed.
scope: Continuously, not from a static inventory

Critically, the claims core is not internet-facing — confirmed, which is exactly what you want to verify each morning.
