scenarios.impact: Unintended entry point outside change control · possible data path
scenarios.body: A dev API that shouldn’t be public is exactly what attacker reconnaissance looks for — it’s outside change control, likely under-hardened, and may reach internal data. It should be pulled offline today; it is the highest-priority of the three flags.

scenarios.impact: Subdomain takeover · phishing under your own brand
scenarios.body: An unmanaged subdomain pointing at a deprovisioned service can be claimed by an attacker and used to host phishing under your trusted domain — turning your own brand into the lure. This compounds the live phishing campaign.

ciso-attacksurface.tells: What an attacker sees when they look at you. The number to act on is the 3 flagged — especially the dev API. This is also where the unpatched-vuln risk becomes reachable: attack surface × unpatched critical is how external breaches actually start.

ciso-posture.claim: Overall security posture — how the 82 is computed
ciso-posture.what: What the posture score is, exactly how the 82 is calculated from measured domain scores, and why it isn’t higher. This is a roll-up of evidence — not an analyst’s opinion.
scope: Nine security domains, each scored from live evidence
The weight each domain carries in the roll-up
The two domains dragging the score down
ciso-posture.signals: 82 = weighted average of nine domain scores, each computed from live telemetry and tested controls. Change the evidence and the number moves; no one types in an 82.
ciso-posture.why: It is 82, not higher, because two domains pull the weighted average down: Recovery & resilience (66) and AI governance (52). The strong domains — identity, endpoint, detection — would put posture near 88 on their own, but recovery and AI governance are weighted in and drag it to 82. The +4 this quarter came from identity (MFA rollout) and endpoint (coverage) gains.

ciso-posture.tells: The one number the board tracks — but it decomposes to exactly which domains earn it and which two are holding it at 82 instead of 88. It tells you precisely where to invest to move it: recovery testing and AI governance, in that order of weight.

ciso-regreadiness.claim: Regulatory readiness — how the 91% is computed
ciso-regreadiness.what: What regulatory readiness measures, how the 91% is derived per regime, and exactly what the missing 9% is. It answers: if a regulator or auditor asked today, could we produce current evidence?
ciso-regreadiness.signals: 91% = the share of in-scope regulatory obligations that have current, evidenced controls and preserved documentation. Computed from control evidence, not a self-assessment survey.
ciso-regreadiness.why: It is 91%, not 100%, and the 9% gap is named, not vague: HIPAA encryption coverage is 98% (not universal), the SEC materiality runbook is current but the last tabletop was 7 months ago, and one PCI control is mid-remediation. These are in-flight, owned items — not unknowns or failures.

ciso-regreadiness.tells: Whether the company could defend itself on paper today. 91% means yes on the overwhelming majority, with the 9% being specific, assigned, in-progress items you can name to a regulator — which is itself a defensible posture.

questions.a: Expected annualized loss. The 95th-percentile (Cyber VaR) is $156M, over the $120M appetite at the tail. $94M is within; the tail is not.

questions.q: What is $94M in business terms?
questions.a: About 0.51% of revenue — roughly 23 days of operating income. That translation is what makes it a board number, not a security number.

scope: Every business area carrying modeled material exposure
ciso-exposure.signals: Aggregate of per-area modeled exposure. The headline finding is concentration: one area carries almost all of it.
ciso-exposure.why: $94M is driven overwhelmingly by claims processing (a single-event modeled loss of $94M), with AI-assisted claims ($12–40M) the fastest-rising. Member portal and payments are immaterial by comparison. Exposure is concentrated, not diffuse — which is good news, because it means it’s actionable.
ciso-exposure.detailLabel: Where the exposure sits — by area
ciso-exposure.aggregate: The material exposure is concentrated in claims — one area carries it. That is why claims modernization is the single highest-leverage funding decision: fund it down and the aggregate drops materially, not marginally.

scenarios.body: AI/agentic and third-party concentration keep rising while PAM and recovery lag. The $94M creeps upward quarter over quarter — the slow version of the same loss.

ceo-bizrisk.what: Whether the company’s aggregate cyber risk sits within the risk appetite the board has set. “In tolerance” is not a feeling — it means we are under the line on every appetite measure the board approved.

questions.q: In tolerance against whose appetite — under every limit?
questions.a: Against the board-approved $120M appetite. Aggregate residual ($94M) is under it with $26M headroom — though one contributor (claims) is over its own sub-line.

questions.q: What would take us out of tolerance?
questions.a: A single uncontained claims event, or correlated contributors — which pushes the tail (VaR $156M) over. "In tolerance" is true on expected loss, tight at the tail.

questions.q: Can I tell investors "under control" and defend it?
questions.a: Yes, defensibly — tested controls, named gaps, documented decisions. Boards now face Caremark duty-of-care scrutiny, so the evidence trail is the point.

questions.q: How does cyber compare to our other enterprise risks?
questions.a: Shown apples-to-apples in annualized-loss dollars with market, credit and operational risk. Cyber is currently the 3rd-largest enterprise risk by residual.

ceo-bizrisk.signals: Tolerance test: residual annualized loss ≤ appetite AND no uncontained material event AND 0 disclosure triggers. All three must hold to read “in tolerance.”
ceo-bizrisk.why: We are in tolerance because we sit under the board’s line on every measure: modeled residual annualized loss is $94M against a $120M appetite; the one elevated exposure (claims) is on a verified compensating control, so there is no uncontained material event; and zero events meet the disclosure threshold. The moment any one of these crosses, this tile flips and names which line broke.

scenarios.t: Claims compensating control fails before the path is closed

scenarios.t: Third-party (NASCO) risk drifts further over appetite

scenarios.body: NASCO is a single-source PHI processor with no alternate. scenarios.body: AI-assisted claims makes model decisions on PHI with no human oversight. An ungoverned decision that exposes PHI would add a second uncontained material exposure — two at once would put aggregate residual clearly over appetite and trigger board notification.

ceo-bizrisk.aggregate: If two of these hit together (e.g. claims control fails while NASCO drifts), modeled residual would exceed the $120M appetite and at least one uncontained material event would exist — the company would be out of tolerance, triggering board notification and a posture change. ceo-bizrisk.tells: “In tolerance” is the one word that lets the CEO tell the board cyber risk is being held inside the limits they set. It is defensible because it names the thresholds and shows the headroom — and it will flip the instant a limit is crossed, naming the cause.

exp-ai.claim: AI-Assisted Claims — why it ranks High (rising fastest)
exp-ai.what: Why AI-assisted claims is a High business risk and the fastest-growing exposure in the company — in business terms, not model terms.
scope: Models making decisions that touch 2.4M PHI records
Agentic AI with production tool access
exp-ai.signals: Ranking = impact × likelihood × governance gap. AI scores High because it makes unsupervised decisions on PHI with essentially no governance — and the surface is growing faster than any other.
exp-ai.why: High because all three drivers are elevated and worsening: (1) impact — models make decisions on PHI that can wrongly approve or deny claims at scale; (2) likelihood — there is no human oversight and no AI standard implemented, so an ungoverned error or abuse is a matter of when; (3) trajectory — developer, agentic and shadow AI are being adopted faster than governance can catch up. It is the only risk rising on every driver at once.

exp-ai.aggregate: Worst realistic case combines a mass mis-adjudication with a shadow-AI PHI leak: $12–40M modeled loss, an EU AI Act high-risk classification on the claims model, unfair-claims regulatory exposure, and reprocessing cost. None is governed today — which is the entire basis for funding enterprise AI governance now, before the surface grows further.

exp-portal.claim: Member Portal — why it ranks Medium
exp-portal.what: Why the member portal is a Medium risk — high attack volume but contained consequence — defended as a deliberate rating, not neglect.
scope: Member account data (not the claims core)
exp-portal.signals: Ranking = impact × likelihood × recoverability. Portal is Medium because likelihood is high but impact is contained and recovery is strong — high volume, low consequence.
exp-portal.why: Medium, not High, because the drivers point in different directions: likelihood is high (internet-facing, constant credential-stuffing pressure), but impact is contained (no path to the claims core or mass PHI; worst case is account-level data and brand), and recoverability is strong (multi-region, fast failover). A High-volume, low-consequence risk is correctly a Medium — and saying so is how the rating stays credible.

exp-payments.claim: Provider Payments — why it ranks Low
exp-payments.what: Why provider payments is a Low risk — and why “Low” here is an evidenced, defensible rating rather than complacency.
scope: Shared dependency on the claims / NASCO ecosystem
exp-payments.signals: Ranking = impact × likelihood × recoverability — all three favorable. The only elevated factor is contagion from the claims ecosystem it shares.
exp-payments.why: Low because every driver is favorable: no open exposure path (likelihood low), bounded and insured impact, and recovery under a day (multi-region, well-segmented). scenarios.impact: Concentrated provider impact in the highest-volume window
scenarios.body: An outage during the month-end disbursement peak concentrates impact on the most providers at once — more reputational than financial, but timing amplifies it.

cro-tpr.claim: Third-party concentration — why it’s drifting to the appetite line
cro-tpr.what: Why third-party (vendor) risk is drifting toward the board’s appetite line — the concentration problem behind it, in enterprise terms.

questions.q: Drifting toward or past appetite — and what’s driving it?
questions.a: Drifting toward the line, not past. The driver is concentration: NASCO is a single-source PHI processor with no alternate, and 2 of 14 critical vendors dropped a rating tier.

questions.q: Do critical vendors meet SLAs / hold current SOC 2?
questions.a: 12 of 14 do; the 2 that slipped are the drift. NASCO holds SOC 2, but its single-source status is the unmanaged risk, not its attestation.

questions.q: Does a vendor failure remove our failover?
questions.a: Yes — a NASCO outage or breach removes the failover for the $94M claims exposure. The direct vendor dollar ($0.4M) understates it; concentration multiplies the biggest risk.

scope: NASCO — single-source PHI claims processor (no alternate)
cro-tpr.signals: Drifting because two critical vendors’ ratings fell and the most critical one — NASCO — has no alternate provider. Concentration, not any single vendor, is the core problem.
cro-tpr.why: It is drifting toward appetite because the company’s most critical PHI processor (NASCO) is single-source with no failover, two of fourteen critical vendors dropped a rating tier this quarter, and tier-2 vendors aren’t continuously monitored. The dollar figure looks small in isolation — the danger is that concentration multiplies the claims exposure rather than adding to it.
cro-tpr.detailLabel: The real impact to the business

scenarios.t: NASCO suffers a breach or outage
scenarios.impact: Claims can’t process or fail over · PHI exposed via the processor · org liable as covered entity
scenarios.body: As a single-source PHI processor with no alternate, a NASCO breach or outage stops claims with nowhere to fail over to, and exposes PHI through the processor — for which the company remains liable as the covered entity. This is the concentration risk that makes the $94M claims exposure un-recoverable on the timeline that matters.

scenarios.impact: Compounded exposure as both critical vendors degrade together
scenarios.body: The two already-drifting critical vendors degrade in the same window. Individually manageable; together they push aggregate third-party risk over the appetite line and strain the same response team at once.

scenarios.impact: Indirect PHI exposure that’s hard to see or scope
scenarios.body: A subcontractor four parties deep is breached. PHI exposure flows back through the chain, but with no continuous monitoring below tier-1 it’s detected late and is hard to scope — extending notification timelines.

cro-tpr.aggregate: The direct dollar figure ($0.4M) understates the real risk: concentration means a single vendor event removes the failover for the company’s #1 exposure. That coupling is why third-party risk is the quiet driver behind claims — and why continuous vendor monitoring is the decision on the table.
cro-tpr.tells: Why a “small” third-party number is actually the lever that makes the biggest risk worse — and why it can’t be judged in isolation.

cro-identity.claim: Identity & access — why it’s Low and improving
cro-identity.what: Why identity & access risk is Low and improving — a defensible rating that still names its one live thread.
scope: The privileged path to the claims database
cro-identity.signals: Low and improving: MFA coverage is high and rising, phishing-resistant auth is rolling out. The one residual is privileged access — and it’s the thread that ties to the #1 risk.
cro-identity.why: Low because workforce identity is strongly controlled (98.1% MFA, phishing-resistant auth rolling out) and improving quarter over quarter. It is not rated “None” because one privileged-access gap remains — the PAM rollout at 60% — and that gap is the same privileged path that makes the claims exposure exploitable. Identity is mostly solved; its one live thread runs straight to claims.
cro-identity.detailLabel: The real impact to the business

scenarios.impact: Account compromise → lateral movement
scenarios.body: Attackers find and target the small residual of accounts without phishing-resistant MFA. A single compromise becomes a foothold for lateral movement — the standard breach entry point.

scenarios.t: A privileged credential is abused before PAM closes the gap
scenarios.impact: This is the bridge to the claims ransomware path
scenarios.body: The 40% of privileged access not yet under PAM is exactly the gap that lets an attacker reach the claims database. Identity’s one unfinished control is the enabler of the company’s #1 exposure — which is why the PAM rollout is funded and tracked.

scenarios.impact: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing attacks resume
scenarios.body: If the phishing-resistant rollout loses momentum, the org stays exposed to MFA-fatigue and push-bombing techniques that defeat basic MFA — reversing the improvement trend.

cro-identity.aggregate: Identity is genuinely well-controlled and improving — but its one open thread (privileged access) is the bridge to the claims exposure. Closing PAM is what turns this from “Low with a live thread” into simply Low.
cro-identity.tells: A defensible Low that doesn’t pretend to be zero — it names the one privileged-access thread that connects identity to the biggest risk.

cro-aggregate.claim: Aggregate enterprise risk — why it’s within appetite
cro-aggregate.what: How the whole enterprise’s cyber risk sums across all six leaders, and why the total sits within the board’s appetite even with one contributor over its own line.

questions.q: Within by how much — expected or tail?
questions.a: Aggregate residual is under the $120M appetite on expected loss, with $26M headroom. The 95th-percentile (Cyber VaR) is $156M — over at the tail. “Within” is true on expected, tight at the tail.

questions.q: Does it assume the contributors are independent?
questions.a: Yes — that’s the fragility. The model treats claims, third-party and AI as partly independent. If one event correlates them (claims → NASCO → AI), the aggregate crosses appetite. Concentration, not the sum, is the risk.

questions.q: Is this a “green dashboard” illusion?
questions.a: No — the control indicators behind it are validated, and one contributor (claims) is shown over its line rather than hidden. A roll-up that showed all-green while claims breached would be the illusion; this one names it.

cro-aggregate.signals: Within appetite because aggregate residual sits under the $120M line even though one contributor (claims) is over its own — diversification holds the total. The watch is correlation.
cro-aggregate.why: Within appetite because the contributions sum to a residual under the $120M board line, and the contributors are treated as partly independent — so one over-line item (claims) doesn’t breach the whole. The fragility, and the reason this is “within” rather than “comfortable,” is correlation: the model assumes claims, third-party and AI move independently, and they may not.

scenarios.t: Correlated event breaks the diversification assumption
scenarios.impact: Independent-looking contributors move as one → aggregate blows past appetite
scenarios.body: A claims incident triggers NASCO (third-party) and exposes the ungoverned AI model in the same event. The contributors the model treated as independent move together — and the aggregate that looked “within” crosses the $120M appetite. Correlation is the hidden risk in any aggregation.

scenarios.t: AI keeps growing as a share of the total
scenarios.impact: AI becomes the top contributor within a year — ungoverned
scenarios.body: AI/agentic risk is already 16% and rising fastest. Left ungoverned, it becomes the single largest contributor within a year, shifting the whole risk distribution toward the least-controlled domain.

scenarios.t: A second contributor crosses its own appetite line
scenarios.impact: Two over-line items at once → aggregate out of tolerance
scenarios.body: If third-party or operational risk crosses its line while claims is still over, two simultaneous over-appetite contributors push the aggregate out of tolerance and force a board-level posture change.

cro-aggregate.aggregate: The enterprise is within appetite today — but on a diversification assumption that a single correlated event could break, and against an AI contribution growing every quarter. “Within” is true now and fragile to correlation, which is the sophisticated read the risk committee should carry.
cro-aggregate.tells: Why “within appetite” is a real answer the CRO can give the board today — and exactly what would flip it, so it’s held honestly rather than assumed.
cro-aggregate.confidence: Medium-High · correlation assumptions are the soft spot ◐

cio-svc.what: Real-time operational status of the services the business has defined as mission-critical. If any one is down, members can’t transact, claims stop, or money can’t move.

questions.q: Up fully, or degraded / on workarounds?
questions.a: All 9 mission-critical services are up. Claims is running on a compensating control after today's contained event — functioning, but named rather than hidden behind a green light.

questions.q: Can they keep running if a provider fails?
questions.a: For most, yes — with failover. The exception is NASCO (single-source claims/PHI processor) with no alternate; that's the concentration the CRO tracks.

questions.q: Do we know how our providers behave when everything goes wrong?
questions.a: Tier-1 providers have tested failover; the gap is fourth-party dependencies below tier-1, which aren't continuously monitored.

cio-svc.signals: A service reads “up” only when its health check is green AND its last 60-second synthetic transaction succeeded — not on a ping alone.
cio-svc.why: All 9 services returning healthy; every service’s last synthetic passed within the last 60 seconds; 0 service-down incidents open. Claims Processing is up on a verified compensating control (flagged amber), not down — the tile never hides that inside a green.

scenarios.impact: Claims stop with nowhere to fail over
scenarios.body: The single-source PHI processor goes down. Claims cannot process and there is no alternate — the concentration risk turns "Up" into a hard stop on the $2.3M/hr path.

scenarios.t: Compensating control fails on the contained event
scenarios.impact: Today’s held event reactivates
scenarios.body: The compensating control holding today’s incident fails. The contained event reopens and claims degrade — the green light was conditional, and the condition broke.

scenarios.impact: A sub-provider below tier-1 takes a service down
scenarios.body: A dependency four parties deep — unmonitored — fails and cascades up. A service shows degraded with no obvious cause because visibility stops at tier-1.

cio-svc.aggregate: If realized, "Up" becomes a claims-stopping outage, most likely through the NASCO single-source dependency — which is why concentration, not the green light, is the real status.
cio-svc.tells: The “are we open for business” answer in one glance — claims flowing, members served, payments moving. If one service degraded, this tile names which; it never aggregates a failure into a green.

cio-uptime.what: Availability of the same 9 critical services over the trailing 30 days, measured against the service-level objective (SLO target 99.95%).

questions.q: Which systems — the critical ones, or an average that hides them?
questions.a: The same 9 critical services, measured against a 99.95% SLO — not a blended estate average. 99.98% is above target.

questions.q: What did the 0.02% cost?
questions.a: About 8.6 minutes of degradation in the window, itemized by service. No member-facing outage; the cost was internal, not revenue.

questions.q: Is this a trend or a snapshot?
questions.a: Trailing 30 days, reported as a trend, not a point-in-time. Reliability direction is tracked separately so a good month can't mask a bad slope.

cio-uptime.signals: Availability = in-scope service-minutes minus measured downtime, divided by total minutes, over 30 days.
cio-uptime.why: 99.98% over 30 days equals about 8.6 minutes of total downtime — and every minute is attributed: a 6.0-minute Provider Portal outage on the 14th during a database failover, plus 2.6 minutes of planned-maintenance overrun on the 22nd. “Not 100%” is a fact with a named cause, not a mystery.

scenarios.t: A critical service consumes the whole error budget
scenarios.impact: 99.98% masks one service at 99.5%
scenarios.body: The blended number hides a single critical service eating its entire error budget. The average looks healthy while claims or payments quietly breaches its SLO — which is why per-service, not blended, is what matters.

scenarios.t: A short outage lands in the peak claims window
scenarios.impact: 8 minutes at the wrong time = real revenue
scenarios.body: The same minutes that cost nothing overnight cost real money at peak. Uptime percent without timing understates business impact.

scenarios.t: Trend reverses after a good month
scenarios.impact: 99.98% this month, sliding next
scenarios.body: A quiet month flatters the number; a change-heavy month reverses it. A point-in-time figure can mask a worsening slope — which is why direction is tracked separately.

cio-uptime.aggregate: If realized, a healthy-looking 99.98% hides a critical service breaching SLO or downtime at peak — which is why uptime is reported per-service and as a trend, not a blended snapshot.
cio-uptime.tells: Whether you’re honoring the availability commitment to members, providers, and regulators. 99.98% against a 99.95% SLO sits comfortably in band, with the headroom visible — and the lost minutes accounted for.

cio-recovery.what: How confidently the critical services could be recovered within their target RTO/RPO if they failed today — a composite of backup success, restore-test recency, failover validation, and runbook currency. This is forward resilience, distinct from uptime, which is past availability.

questions.q: When was recovery last tested, on what, and what happened?
questions.a: The last full failover test was 142 days ago — overdue. Measured restore was 4.3 days against a 4-hour RTO for claims. That gap is why this reads 78%, not higher.

questions.q: Proven under pressure, or only on paper?
questions.a: Partly on paper — which is the problem. A backup "success" log isn't proof a system boots; the 78% reflects unproven restores, not just missing backups.

questions.q: Are the RTOs real, and is the fix funded?
questions.a: Until re-tested, the RTOs are aspirational. Recovery modernization ($6.0M) is funded and is one of the two board decisions — the single biggest posture lever.

cio-recovery.signals: Five inputs scored per service: last successful backup · last successful restore test · last DR failover test · measured RTO/RPO vs target · runbook last updated.
cio-recovery.why: The 22-point gap is named, not hand-waved. The biggest drags: the Claims DB’s last full DR failover test was 142 days ago against a ≤90-day target, and the Provider Portal’s last restore took 4.3 days against a 4-hour RTO. Each deduction carries its weight, so the score is auditable down to the failing test.
detail: Claims DB · last DR failover test
2 services · backed up, no validated restore (6 mo)

scenarios.impact: 4.3-day restore vs 4-hour RTO
scenarios.body: Claims is hit and must be recovered now, before the overdue DR test. Restore takes 4.3 days against a 4-hour RTO — a multi-day, ~$72M/day outage because recovery was unproven.

scenarios.t: Backups restore but the system will not boot
scenarios.impact: "Success" logs, failed recovery
scenarios.body: Backups report success but the restored system does not come up — the gap a success log hides. Readiness was 78% precisely because boot-level restore was not verified.

scenarios.t: Recovery depends on a compromised dependency
scenarios.impact: Identity or NASCO is down when needed to recover
scenarios.body: Recovery needs identity or the processor, which are themselves impaired in the incident. The recovery path breaks because a dependency was not independent.

cio-recovery.aggregate: If realized, the unproven 22% is exactly what turns an incident into a multi-day outage — which is why an overdue DR test makes documented RTOs aspirational, and why recovery is a funded board decision.
cio-recovery.tells: The “if ransomware hit tonight, how sure are we we’d be back in time?” number. 78% is real exposure, and it points at the exact tests to run to close it — which is why it feeds directly into the costed recovery-modernization decision.
cio-recovery.freshness: As of last backup/test records · oldest input 142d old
cio-recovery.confidence: High · from backup & DR systems · restore times partly manual ◐

cio-sev1.what: Count of currently-open Severity-1 incidents — defined as a member-facing outage, PHI exposure, or revenue-stopping event — across the critical services.

questions.q: Zero now, or zero this period?
questions.a: Zero open right now. Today's claims event was contained below Sev-1, and the last true Sev-1 was recovered within MTTR. "Zero" is current state, not a clean history.

questions.q: What dependency would break recovery if one hit?
questions.a: The watch items are identity (privileged access to claims) and NASCO — either can turn a Sev-1 into a recovery problem rather than a quick restore.

questions.q: Who can declare a disaster, and is that decided in advance?
questions.a: Yes — the incident commander and CIO have pre-agreed declaration authority, so the call isn't argued at 2 a.m. while revenue bleeds.

scope: Live incident queue for the 9 critical services, classified against the documented Sev-1 severity matrix

cio-sev1.why: Nothing currently meets Sev-1 criteria. The last Sev-1 was 11 days ago (claims-gateway latency), resolved in 47 minutes. If this were greater than 0, the drawer would list each incident and link straight to its ticket.

scenarios.t: Today’s contained event escalates to Sev-1
scenarios.impact: "0" flips to an active member-facing outage
scenarios.body: The compensating control holding today’s event fails and it crosses the Sev-1 line — member-facing, revenue-stopping. "0 open" is a current state, and current states change.

scenarios.t: A Sev-1 hits while recovery is unproven
scenarios.impact: Incident + 4.3-day restore = prolonged outage
scenarios.body: A Sev-1 lands during the recovery gap. With restore unproven at 4.3 days, a normally-bounded incident becomes a multi-day event.

scenarios.t: Disaster-declaration authority is unclear in the moment
scenarios.impact: Time lost deciding who calls it
scenarios.body: Despite pre-agreed authority, a novel incident sits in a grey zone and minutes are lost. The cost of a Sev-1 is set in the first hour.

cio-sev1.aggregate: If realized, "0 open" becomes an active Sev-1 whose damage is set by recovery readiness and decision speed — which is why the zero is reported with its dependencies, not alone.
cio-sev1.tells: The real-time “is anything on fire right now” reading. Read it alongside Recovery Readiness: 0 Sev-1s says calm now; 78% says not yet ready for the worst. Two different questions, two separate tiles — never merged.

cio-change.what: The risk being introduced by changes (deployments, config, infrastructure) to critical services in the current window — a function of change volume × blast radius × historical failure rate × freeze status. A leading indicator: it’s about what you’re about to break.
scope: All changes in the last/next 7 days touching the 9 critical services, by type (standard / normal / emergency), plus the change-freeze calendar
cio-change.signals: Risk rises with volume, blast radius and historical failure rate; it falls with CAB approval and freeze adherence.
cio-change.why: 3 standard changes this week, all CAB-approved, none touching the NASCO claims core; change-failure rate 4% (healthy band); 0 emergency changes; last rollback verified clean. It flips to High the moment a high-blast-radius change to the claims core enters the window unreviewed — and names it.
cio-change.tells: You asked what the value is: self-inflicted change is the #1 cause of outages. Every other tile is backward-looking; this one is forward-looking — it tells you whether tomorrow’s outage is being created by today’s deployment, in time to stop it. The only tile that prevents rather than reports.

cio-trend.what: The direction of reliability over time — a composite trajectory of uptime, MTTR, change-failure rate and incident frequency across the last six months. A direction, not a single point.

questions.q: Up over what horizon — or just a quiet month?
questions.a: A six-month composite of uptime, MTTR, change-failure rate and incident frequency — a direction, not a single point. The slope is genuinely up.

questions.q: Are our resilience investments actually reducing downtime/MTTR?
questions.a: Yes on uptime and MTTR; the laggard is recovery (the 4.3-day restore), which is exactly what the funded modernization targets.

questions.q: Does this satisfy board-level (DORA-style) resilience accountability?
questions.a: It's structured for it — tested, trend-based, board-reported. The one open item to fully satisfy it is the overdue DR test.

scope: Rolling 6-month history of the in-scope reliability metrics across the 9 critical services
cio-trend.signals: A net verdict computed from four time-series; any deteriorating signal is listed honestly, not hidden behind the arrow.
cio-trend.why: MTTR is down from 95 to 62 minutes over 6 months; change-failure rate down from 9% to 4%; incident frequency down about 30%. The one signal still moving the wrong way — recovery readiness at 78% vs the 90% target — is shown, so “Up” is a net verdict you can inspect, not a cheerful arrow.

scenarios.t: Recovery drags the trend back down
scenarios.impact: The one laggard reverses the gain
scenarios.body: Uptime and MTTR improve, but the unfixed 4.3-day recovery causes a major outage that erases quarters of gains. The trend is only as strong as its weakest component.

scenarios.t: Change-failure rate spikes on a big release
scenarios.impact: A heavy change window reverses the slope
scenarios.body: A large release pushes change-failure rate up and incidents with it. The improving line bends the wrong way for a quarter.

scenarios.t: Improvement plateaus before the resilience bar
scenarios.impact: Trend flattens with the DR test still open
scenarios.body: Gains plateau while the overdue DR test keeps resilience short of the board/DORA bar. Up is not the same as sufficient.

cio-trend.aggregate: If realized, the improving trend reverses on its weakest link — recovery — which is why the direction is reported with the open DR test named, not as an unqualified arrow.
cio-trend.tells: You asked what it helps the C-suite with: a single good month (99.98%) can sit on top of a worsening trajectory. The trend answers the board’s real question — are our reliability investments working, and should we keep funding them? It separates a lucky month from genuine, fundable improvement.
